O sweet to be A politician Whose acts are all Above suspicion But who can always Find a way To make his nuisance Value pay.
That is the way the people are looking at the Beauharnois scandal, and unless everybody is to be smirched by the disclosures we had better take no uncertain stand in the matter.
The Beauharnois committee was also told something about campaign funds. It is interesting to know where some of the campaign funds came from. It would be equally interesting to know where the remainder came from for both parties; because I do not think campaign funds always go to one party, J. fancy they go to both. It is not so long ago that we had the liquor scandal, when an investigation disclosed that huge sums were paid to both parties by the liquor interests; then we had the customs scandal, and now the Beauharnois scandal. These investigations have given us three little glimpses of how campaign funds are paid. This does not mean that we know where all the campaign funds come from, but in the latest disclosures John Aird, jr., put it very well indeed. He said: "Gratefulness was always regarded as an important factor in dealing with democratic governments."

Yes, but he was telling what Aird told him. Well, in one way I do not blame the parties, I blame the people for payment of campaign funds. As long as the people enjoy having corporations and bunches of rogues, or whatever you like to call them 

I do not mean that all corporations are controlled by rogues, I am thinking of this particular gang-as long as the people enjoy being fooled by men of that type it is their own fault. During my own campaigns I have said this many times: If the people of Southeast Grey do not want to pay for the financing of a candidate, then don't have one; if they do want one, then pay for it. Suppose every family in Canada paid Si to the candidate of his choice, that is money enough to carry on an honest campaign, to pay for radio broadcasts, newspaper advertisements, lectures, and any other decent method

Beauharnois Power-Report

of convincing the electorate of the virtues of the candidate. Until they do that we shall go on from the customs and the Beauharnois scandals to other scandals, on, on, on, endlessly, and sometimes it will be the Conservatives who are pure and holy, and sometimes-if they are careful and astute-it will be the Liberals.
Undoubtedly the methods of securing campaign funds for the support of the old parties throttles the whole idea of democratic government. The large sums which the old parties get-and they are not 25 cent pieces, I should judge-cause them to be "grateful," in the words of John Aird, jr., to those who give the money. However much those who require such campaign funds may try to be perfectly honest in their relation to the people of Canada, they can scarcely help being biased in favour of those who made their election possible by their bounty.
In the same issue of Saturday Night there is a very interesting cartoon, and I hope all hon. members will look at it. "The People" shown by a figure in the centre, very much bedraggled, a beaten little man, with a bump on his forehead, a black eye, hair dishevelled, deprived of his coat and in a state of impotent rage, his fists clenched, while on his right hand are two grinning, well-dressed, corpulent gentlemen representing the power interests, on his left two financiers emptying his coat pockets, in the background two politicians -there should be three-slinking off with a fat bag, seeming a bit ashamed. The cartoon is headed: They've Taken Everything but His Vote. And that is about where we are in democratic government. The people can vote, but they cannot do much else, for it does not matter a great deal which side they vote for. True, a change of government does help; we find out what the other party was doing, and that is always interesting. But certainly if there were no big campaign funds available to the old parties the number of independent members in this house would be much greater. They might not be sitting in this corner; they might not think as we do but they would be independent, free men, and how they would enjoy it. I am sure, during the last few weeks, many men in this house have gone through what the right hon. leader of the opposition last night called the valley of humiliation.
Then there is something else I should like to know. I should like to know why Sweezey gave John Aird that $125,000. The fact that it went to the province which supplied the contract which enabled the company to sell bonds is, to me, a suspicious circumstance.

Then take Aird's own words as given by Mr. Sweezey-we will go over them again. He testified that Aird said:
That he thought that a contribution would be in order to the Ontario Conservative party because we would probably be having a lot more dealings with the Ontario people, and that gratefulness was always regarded as an important factor in dealing with democratic governments.
The matter is pretty clear to anyone who is not too credulous, but we ought to know more than we know about it as yet. One is almost led to suspect that long years of careful manoeuvring have taught certain people how to completely cover their tracks. I am not sure that the committee went into that question as far as they might have; I am not sure why it was not made clearer, though of course in the minds of the people it ,'s quite clear. Mr. Aird was certainly a marvellous man to get that amount of money for a few words of advice, the nature of which he could not recall. Advice must be valuable.
Before I finish-and I have not taken very long, nor do I intend to do so

I must say that I think the people of Canada ought to take this lesson seriously in regard to campaign funds. If they do so this revelation will be worth while; a great lesson will have been learned by this investigation. I am sure I do not enjoy seeing people's characters besmirched, but there was one individual, Senator McDougald, about whom I feel it would not matter very much. A man who not only used his position of trust for his own enrichment but who betrayed his best friend seems to me beyond anything but our contempt. All the others, I suppose, are doing just what is being done in other corporations day after day and month after month, which goes to show how absolutely rotten is the social system under which we live. The Toronto Saturday Night, which is not a radical publication, or was not such, in P.M.R.'s column says the following:
If the capitalistic system is to survive, there must not be scandals like the Beauharnois. Disclosures such as those which have shocked the country in recent weeks are just so much ammunition for the reds.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Leader of the Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: POWER TO DEAL WITH AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS AND LABOUR SITUATION-MAINTENANCE OF ORDER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, since I have had an opportunity of seeing the bill I must confess that I feel it lends emphasis to the remarks I made in speaking on the resolution upon which the bill is based, and that it really would be impossible to express in too emphatic terms the objections to which the measure as proposed is open.
I should like to repeat that I believe it is a very great mistake to associate the relief of unemployment arising from economic causes, of which existing fiscal policies are one, and the relief required in rural areas because of distress occasioned by drought, failure of harvest and other like causes. It is an even greater and graver mistake to associate these relief measures with a measure concerned with peace, order and good government in Canada, which looks to me like a war measure applied to our country in times of peace. One would think that the possibility of a civil war were contemplated in this country by a measure of this kind, and that it was going to arise out of the extent of unemployment.
That is most unfortunate. The Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) did say that he desired legislation with respect to peace, order and good government in order to deal more effectively with some noisy minority who might represent certain Bolshevist or what he terms communist views which he did not think should be permitted to make headway in this
country, but the public will not get that idea from this measure, nor will those who are suffering from unemployment and who are experiencing the great distress which is theirs in virtue of the fact that, seek as they will, they are unable at the present time to secure remunerative emplojunent. That is my first objection.
There is another objection, which is perhaps even stronger. The bill gives to the governor in council power not only to spend money for certain purposes but to borrow money and spend it without limit. I confess, Mr. Speaker, that I do not believe there will be found on the statutes of this parliament any comparable measure in the whole history of Canadian legislation. As was pointed out the other evening by the hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Bourassa), when parliament was asked to vote huge sums to meet the emergencies and necessities of war, the Prime Minister of the day never thought of coming to this House of Commons and asking parliament to give him a blank cheque for the purpose. He fixed some amount. True he was unable to estimate within appreciable bounds what the amount might be that would ultimately be required, but, notwithstanding, he did have some regard for the rights of parliament. It seems to me this bill disregards parliament altogether; it is a complete usurpation of the rights of parliament. This afternoon my right hon. friend spoke with some force, some emphasis and feeling about having regard to the traditions and the institutions of government. Well, the fundamental tradition in all that pertains to responsible government is that the people's representatives in the House of Commons must exercise control over taxation and that that right must never be taken away from
them.	It -cannot be too strongly emphasized that that is exactly what this bill does. It takes away from this House of Commons and this parliament control over taxation, because no amount is named. We have no knowledge whatever of how much will be borrowed and how much will be spent. All we know is that after the treasury has been depleted to a very considerable extent, and our public debt has been correspondingly increased, and not until
then,	will the people have any idea of what this particular measure involves. I do not
_ think it is possible to emphasize too strongly how serious is the departure which the government is making in asking this house, no matter what the reason may be, to give it unlimited powers of the kind.
When one reads the measure and contemplates the possible uses of the moneys,

Farm and Unemployment Relief
judging from the provisions with respect to what the governor in council may -do once these powers are given, the situation will be seen to be more serious than ever. It becomes, I confess, extremely grave. In the first place, the measure gives the government power to aid in the relief of unemployment in a manner similar to that which characterized the legislation passed at the special session and which seemed at the time to be going pretty far. But it gives the government wider powers than were conferred at that time. Such relief as was given at the special session had relation to the needs of the provinces and the municipalities, and to a corresponding contribution on their part, which surrounded possible expenditures with some sort of limiting safeguard. But see what this measure does. It enables the governor in council to use any sum of money it may wish in order to-
(a)	Provide for the construction, extension or improvement of public works, buildings, undertakings, railways, highways, subways, bridges and canals, harbours and wharves, and any other works and undertakings of any nature or kind whatsoever.
Why have a parliament at all? Why have estimates submitted to parliament for consideration if the governor in council is to be given authority to do without any control by parliament all these things which ought ;o be subject to the most careful scrutiny ff this House of Commons? Take the next power given the ministry under this bill. They are empowered to:
(b)	Assist in defraying the cost of the production, sale and distribution of the products of the field, farm, forest, sea, river and mine.
That gives the government power to do almost anything in the way of subsidizing any industry associated with the great natural resources of the country. They can give moneys to any extent to any enterprise to be used in any way. Why bring in a measure such as the one which passed this house a day or two ago, granting to the farmers a five cent bonus in connection with the production of their grain when under a measure of this kind the government without further sanction by parliament could give them 25? There was no necessity for that measure with thi3 bill in view. All the powers required to grant that assistance and as much more as desired* are being given in this bill to the governor in council without even the necessity of any supervision on the part of parliament. Take the next section, which empowers the government to:

(c)	Assist provinces, cities, towns, municipalities and other bodies or associations, by loaning moneys thereto or guaranteeing repayment of moneys thereby, or in such other manner as may be deemed necessary or advisable.
Contemplate what that means. It give3 the government the right to borrow to any extent, to assist in any way they please, for any purpose, the provinces, the cities and towns and municipalities, and other bodies or associations. That pretty nearly covers all important organizations that can be thought of which would require assistance for any reason whatever.
While the measure has reference to unemployment and farm relief and peace and order-that is the title of the bill-in reality it may be summed up in the first few words of the title: "An act to confer certain powers upon the governor in council." That is the whole purpose of the bill, to give additional powers to the governor in council to go to any length it wishes. Take the next section. This gives the government the power to:
(d)	Take all such other measures as may be deemed necessary or advisable for carrying out the provisions of this act.
That leaves nothing that the government cannot do if it wishes to act under the terms of the bill now before us. I do not think that anything of this kind has ever been introduced in any parliament in any part of the world since there have been representative institutions and responsible government in the different countries. But the bill goes further. It not only contemplates the expenditure of moneys in this way; it gives the government power to make any orders or regulations it may wish to make by reason of the circumstances recited in the preamble. The preamble touches upon peace, order and good government-that cover's pretty much everything; it touches specifically upon unemployment, rural distress and the like.
What this house is being asked to do now is to enable the government of Canada, without any supervision on the part of this parliament, to make any order or regulation whatsoever; this is equivalent to saying that the government may make any law whatsoever which can possibly have a bearing upon conditions in this country during the remainder of this year and until March, 1932. Never was power asked for by any government at any time of any parliament comparable to that which is asked for in this measure. Not only does the bill give the government power to make these various orders and regulations, but it gives power as well to enforce the orders and regulations. And in that connection it goes the length of providing that the govern-

Farm, and Unemployment Relief
ment may make any order it pleases or any regulations, and that they may therefore revoke those orders and regulations. If a mistake has been made in the original order no consideration is to be due those who may have suffered under the order. I cannot conceive of anything more arbitrary, which an autocratic government could seek to possess, than power such as that. If this measure were dealt with as it deserves to be, it would be the duty of this House of Commons to remain in session until the measure was withdrawn. That is the only way in which I believe a free parliament could in the circumstances be expected to maintain the rights of a free people. At this stage of the session we are forced to realize that no matter what we might do in the way of endless discussion the government would not alter this measure in any particular. As I say, under ordinary circumstances it would have been our duty to fight this bill to the last ditch. Where a measure of this kind was in contemplation, it was the duty of the government not to have made it the last measure of the session, but rather the first of all measures that all hon. members might have had a full opportunity of disclosing before it was too late the grave seriousness of this taking away of powers from parliament to be given exclusively to the ministry.

speechtext:
When the house rose at six o'clock I had not intended to say anything on the bill now before us. Had it not been for the attitude of members of the cabinet I should not have spoken. We know the powers they seek to take out of the hands of parliament, and this is not the first time since the general election of July 28 last, they have endeavoured so to do. We know that at the special session the power of taxation was taken out of the hands of the people, a power which had rested with their representatives in parliament under the terms of the British constitution ever since the days of Magna Charta. The government took the power out of the hands of the representatives of the people and placed it in the hands of one man, the Minister of National Revenue, so that he could place upon goods a value for duty purposes without any respect- whatever to their cost price. He could raise the value as high as he wished, reduce it as low as he wished or change it whenever he wished.
I desire to do nothing to delay the business of the house, but we had before us a few days ago a bill providing that members may be appointed to cabinet positions without asking the sanction of their constituents -just another instance of power being taken out of the hands of the people. The system of representative responsible government under which we live leads us to believe that the people constitute the great tribunal of last resort. That power has been kept in their hands, after having been fought for and won. and has been transmitted to us from the days w-hen the heads of kings used to be tumbled into the wastebasket simply because they persisted in the imposing upon the people of their imperious wills, in the belief that the people were merely the serfs and chattels of the state and that the state and the high command must be all-supreme.

Farm and Unemployment Relief
We have just emerged from the greatest conflict of the ages, and in it the very same principle was at stake, namely whether the common people would rule or whether they were to be serfs and chattels I have already described. In preparing for that great conflict the children of Germany were taken at a very tender age from their mothers and placed in the hands of the military command. So well did they succeed in this way, in building up a great military force that for four long years the freedom and liberty of humanity, the preservation of the liberties of the world, trembled in the balance. The measure which allows cabinet ministers to hold office without appealing to their constituents took away from the people a sacred right which should have been preserved. That is another instance in which the people lost the power and authority which should have been preserved to them.
Here again we have before us a blanket proposition through the medium of which the government can do anything they like with the finances of Canada, and where power is being taken from the representatives of the people and given to the custody of a few. I am not going to obstruct the measure, because I know it will pass, but I did not wish to see it pass without voicing my protest.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not wish to speak at great length on the bill, but I desire to endorse the remarks made in opposition to it and to the manner in which it has been presented to parliament. I support every objection raised by the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) and I am in full sympathy with every word uttered by my hon. friend from Labelle (Mr. Bourassa) in the speech he delivered, which I have read in Hansard.
By this measure the government takes from parliament matters which should be under its exclusive control. It wipes away parliamentary control and takes upon itself all conceivable powers. The terms of the bill I am sure are more general than most people have begun to realize. Referring to section 2, I find the words:
There may be paid out of the consolidated revenue fund such moneys as the governor in council in his discretion may deem expedient to expend for relieving distress, providing employment and maintaining peace, order and good government.
"Peace, order and good government," may mean anything. As was said in committee the other day, the sky is the limit. They are bor-
JMr. T. McMillan.]
rowing the very terms used in the British North America Act to define what is the jurisdiction of the Dominion parliament. Section 91 provides:
It shall be lawful for the queen, by and with the advice and consent of the Senate and the House of Commons, to make laws for the peace, order and good government of Canada, in relation to all matters not coming within the classes of subjects by this act assigned exclusively to the legislatures of the provinces;-
I draw the attention of the house to the following words:
-and for greater certainty, but not so as to restrict the generality of the foregoing terms of this section, it is hereby declared that (notwithstanding anything in this act) the exclusive legislative authority of the parliament of Canada extends to all matters coming within the classes of subjects next hereinafter enumerated, that is to say,-
1.	The public debt and property.
2.	The regulation of trade and commerce.
And so forth. By this bill they borrow not only those words " peace, order and good government," which may mean anything under the sun by way of legislative jurisdiction, but they take the trouble to say in section 3:
Without restricting the generality of the terms of the next preceding section hereof, and notwithstanding the provisions of any statute or law, the governor in council may,-
-do certain things mentioned in paragraphs (a), (b), (c) and (d). Under this bill as now drawn it will be within the power of the governor in council-of the Prime Minister of Canada-to take money from the consolidated revenue fund for the purpose of doing anything which under the British North America Aot this parliament has the right to do. They may establish banks. We do not need any legislation for the completion of the Beau-harnois canal-they will be able to build it under this proposed legislation. And they bring down this measure at the very end of the session, after members on both sides have for five or six months asked the government to define some policy for unemployment; they wait until the very last days of the session and then ask for this wholesale power without any restriction, without any control whatever on the part of parliament. I say that is a piece of despotism which has not had any parallel in the history of Canada, or, so far as I am aware, of any other democratic country enjoying responsible government. It is the establishment of a virtual dictatorship; there is no doubt about it. My hon. friend from Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) said that it smacks of bolshevism, and my hon. friend from Labelle (Mr. Bourassa) said it was fascism. I do not know what term to use to describe it, but it is the worst piece of auto-

Farm and Unemployment Relief
cratic power which a prime minister or a government in this country has ever tried to assume.
Only the other day, Mr. Speaker, when some hon. gentlemen raised the question of unemployment and besought the Prime Minister to define some policy, he said that lie was hampered because of constitutional difficulties, because of the powers of the provinces in matters of property and civil rights, and he had his doubts as to the power of this parliament to intervene directly and not through the provinces. And I myself did say at the time that I thought there was a national emergency, and that if unemployment had become a matter of national emergency the parliament of Canada had the right to legislate with regard to it; but never did it enter my mind, and I do not think it did enter the mind of any hon. gentleman, that that meant that parliament itself would abdicate its control, its power, its jurisdiction, its authority, and entrust all of these into the hands of one man or one set of men, who after all are only a committee of this parliament.
Sir, in matters of national finance the vital principle is the full sovereignty of parliament, of the representatives of the people, in disposing of the burdens which eventually will be borne by their constituents. Parliament and the government must be kept within their respective spheres, or else the whole machinery cannot work. No public money can be taken out of the consolidated revenue fund except by a vote of parliament, either by way of a special statute for an expenditure of a permanent nature like the salaries of judges, members of parliament, or something of that kind, or by an item in the estimates which is voted annually. That is the basic principle of the control of parliament over national expenditures. In the time of the great war at the special session of 1914 I had the honour of a seat in parliament. That was a national emergency; it was war, and in time of war everything seems to be permitted. In all the countries engaged in the war the inevitable answer to every suggestion or criticism was "This is a war measure." But even so the then Prime Minister never thought of asking parliament to give to him what the right hon. gentleman is asking parliament now to entrust to his care. Even then the Prime Minister, Sir Robert Borden, although he asked for votes of money without their being subject to the ordinary measures of control, asked for a definite sum of $50,000,000 at the first session; and at every subsequent session another amount was voted by parliament, but always there was defined
an amount which could not be exceeded, $100,000,000 or $150,000,000; and every time the Prime Minister thought it his duty to give to parliament, to the representatives of the people, a list of the destinations of the money which he was asking parliament to vote. We have nothing of that kind in the present bill. There is no detail; carte blanche is being asked without any control whatever. Even during the war, with the limitations which were then imposed, everybody knows that there were abuses, everybody knows that money was wasted, there were scandals, and a royal commission was appointed. My right hon. friend this afternoon spoke against judges sitting on royal commissions. That was not the idea of the Right Hon. Sir Robert Borden. At the most difficult time of the war when those questions of abuses, of wasted expenditures, of scandals were raised, he appointed two distinguished judges of the land, Right Hon. Mr. Justice Duff, of the Supreme Court of Canada, and Chief Justice Meredith, of Ontario. He thought that was the best way to act, and I quite agree. When there is a question of judicial importance; when judicial powers must be exercised, I agree that judges are the best men to carry on the work. I do not believe in justice being dispensed by majorities belonging to one or another party, and if I may be permitted to use the words of Burke, that is not where we can find the strict neutrality of impartial judges.
I say that even then there were abuses, but in this measure there is no limitation as far as amounts of money are concerned; there is no limitation as to the destination of those moneys or the use to which they may be put. I have been reading a book which my right hon. friend quoted many times when sitting on this side of the house but which he seems to have forgotten since he has been on the other side; I refer to that famous book written by Lord He wart, chief justice of England, entitled The New Despotism. In that book Lord Hewart relates the sitory of an Anglo-Indian civil servant who returned to England on leave after an absence of many years. On arriving in London and while travelling between Victoria and Charing Cross stations he asked the man with him, "What are those buildings?" The man said, "Well, those are the parliament buildings; that is Westminster." The Anglo-Indian said, "What, does that rubbish still go on?" That was the attitude of mind of that gentleman, and if we agree to this bill in its present form I really believe we will be entering on a path fraught with grave danger. Surely someone will say, sometime, "Does this rubbish still go on at Ottawa, the parliament of Canada?"

I contend that the legislation before us is only an aggravation and will disturb the men who consider they have grievances. The only men who were taken care of under the 1930 legislation were the common labourers. The government could go on with a program of building bridges, public buildings and other things of that nature which are really necessary and for the erection of which carpenters, machinists and other artisans could be employed at a fair rate of wages. The hon. member for North Timiskaming (Mr. Bradette), speaking yesterday, complained that some labour members were arguing for higher wages. I have not heard a labour man in the house lodging that argument concerning this kind of work. We urge that fair and reasonable wages be paid.
The regulations under the Unemployment Relief Act of 1930 contained the following clause:
All agreements made with provincial or municipal authorities involving the expenditure of any portion of the money appropriated by the act of public works or undertakings shall contain provisions for the payment of fair wages and hours of work in accordance with the intent of the Fair Wages and Eight-Hour Day Act 1930, and the fair wages policy of the government of Canada as set forth in order in council (P.C. 1206) dated 7th June, 1922, and amendments thereto.
That was the condition under which after the special session the provinces and municipalities received grants. To-night we have the spectacle of the government of Ontario ignoring entirely that provision. The Minister of Labour made the statement that he had by agreement with the province set a fair wage of thirty-five cents an hour, yet we find that in most parts of northern Ontario they were paying only 30 cents an hour. I am going again to ask the government to see to it that the moneys wrongfully withheld from the workingmen of northern Ontario be paid to them. That is an obligation of this government. From a return tabled in response to my inquiry I find that the fair wages for common labour is between 40 to 50 cents an hour, that being the scale set by this government during the last two or three years. Notwithstanding that this scale has recently been reduced to 35 cents an hour, the provincial government is paying only 30 cents an hour. This rate of wages was paid on highway work, and undoubtedly it was

highway robbery to deny the workingmen of northern Ontario the money rightfully coming to them under the provisions of this act of parliament.

Now may I consider, in the light of the present situation in Canada, the situation which existed just over a year ago. At that time a political campaign was being waged throughout the Dominion, and we had the present ministers of the crown making definite and specific promises and pledges to the Canadian people in regard to this grave issue of unemployment. I suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, and to this house that very largely as a result of the promises they made and the pledges they gave they are to-day in office as ministers of the crown. What did my right hon. friend the Prime Minister say? Speaking in his own city of Calgary on June 12, 1930, the Prime Minister said:
This is a new country, and there is no excuse for unemployment in Canada if a government does its duty.
Those words, Mr. Speaker, as and when they were uttered, were either true or false. If they were true, surely we are within the bounds of fair play in confronting the right hon. gentleman, a year after he has been in office, with the promises he made to the

Is there any excuse for Canada to have hard times-if the government is discharging its duty as it should?

The actual situation, sir, which I am sure causes every hon. member of this house the gravest possible concern to-day, is a hundredfold worse than it was before July 28, 1930. And, sir, this legislation is the remedy offered this house; this is the remedy offered the Canadian nation.

Yes; I thought the remarks of hon. gentlemen opposite were pretty cheap when we came here and told them of conditions in the west and they only laughed at us. I have been thirty years in western Canada and have never known things to be so bad. For the last three years in my constituency we have not had a crop. An odd farmer here and there has had seed, but we find poverty and starvation everywhere. I have driven into communities and have talked with people and I can assure the house that I have never known such conditions to exist before. Things are bad enough indeed when a man will come and tell you that his three little girls came to him crying because they had no shoes to wear, nothing to put on their feet to go to a Christmas tree. And when you see a home with five or six little children all with pinched faces, showing starvation, you will realize what things are like. Yet when hon. members come to this house and try to impress upon the government the seriousness of the situation they are only told that they are playing politics.
Just consider what the Prime Minister himself said in regard to conditions out in the west. Speaking in this house he said, as reported at page 779.
The bank reports show that tens of thousands of farmers in western Canada have money in the bank.
And later on, at page 780, he is reported:
There are some people who try to make it appear that the western country is a country that is bankrupt. I repeat, those gentlemen are entirely wrong. Western Canada is the country it always has been.

That was on April 28, 1931. These are some of the things we were told when we tried to put before the government the situation as it has existed out in the west for some time. For three years relief has been handed out. Two years ago that relief was given by the municipalities, and as usual the ne'er-do-wells and drifters, the ordinary labourers and renters, came to the municipality and got relief. But the thrifty farmer who was trying to make a go of it got no consideration. All the relief was handed out and paid for by the municipalities, and the result was that quite often they were very hard up. Last year the relief handed out was paid for partly by this government,' partly by the provincial government, and partly by the municipalities. And, again, those who got relief were the ne'er-do-wells and drifters, the ordinary man who could not succeed; they were always looking for something which they could get as . easily as possible. But the thrifty farmer received little consideration. Yet he had to pay the shot, because one-third was charged to him in his taxes.
What do we find now? This year these thrifty farmers are up against it just as much as anyone else. Their backs are against the wall. They have not paid their loans from the banks for three years; they have not paid their taxes; they are not able to meet the interest on their mortgages. Unless something is done at once for these people they will be driven from the land. There is no doubt about that. Indeed, some are leaving now, and I tell the Prime Minister that this

is a serious condition that must be faced. It is no laughing matter when you see men who are the backbone of the country, thrifty, capable farmers, taking the view that the best thing for them to do is to pull up stakes and move out.
Conditions were so serious in the middle of June, when our pastures are supposed to be good, that horses and cattle were dying from lack of food. In June, in one municipality I know, they brought seventy carloads of hay to keep the stock and cattle alive. Ours are famine conditions, conditions as serious as any that ever existed in India or China when our charitable institutions in this country have raised money for the relief of the people in those countries. Surely we can do the same thing for our own people. If we had hundreds of millions with which to fight the war with Germany, when we were killing and were being killed, surely we have money to spend in western Canada to relieve the people there.

The provincial premier and others had a meeting the other day at \ orkton at which it was stated that this unemployment matter should be handled in a nonpartisan way. I agree with that statement because it is a terrible thing to have to think that a man's politics will determine whether or not he obtains relief. The premier asked his political opponents to join hand in hand with him to meet these conditions. He asked that they do away with politics. One of his ministers got up and asked that politics be forgotten, that we unite to help the unemployed-and then he launched an attack against the opposition. Is that the way to approach an opponent when you want him to join wholeheartedly with you? I say to this government and the government of Saskatchewan that I am ready and willing at all times, to meet them half way to alleviate the condition we have out there. Politics should be forgotten but it must not be expected that we will stand for that sort of treatment. That is not the way a matter such as this should be approached.
The condition is so serious that I do not think any government or group of governments can handle it. The Red Cross and other charitable institutions should be called in to lend their assistance. A government cannot go from home to home and from place to place and hand out boots and shoes and wearing apparel of one kind and another. The charitable organizations will have to be called in to give assistance. Last year while I was in the east I went to several places and called upon certain clergymen, and we sent out two

Farm and Unemployment Relief
ov three tons of second-hand clothing and boots and shoes. That was altogether inadequate even for last winter, which was so mild. If this winter should happen to be a hard winter there will be much suffering unless steps are taken to send help to these people; ten times the amount of clothing will probably be needed. Our charitable organizations should begin at once to make preparations to relieve the suffering of these people in western Canada.
I welcome this bill, but I am sorry that it has come so late in the session. It should have been introduced much earlier in order that this work could have been started some time ago. However, we rejoice over the eleventh hour repentance when it does come.
I think a definite amount should have been named. I believe it will take at least $100,000,000 to relieve conditions. Approximately $80,000,000 was spent last year by our railroads, municipalities and the provincial and dominion governments. The municipalities of western Canada will not have any money to spend this year upon relief; they will not be able to put up a cent. In many of our districts they are threatening to close down the public schools, and that is one objection I have to the grant for technical education. If we are to give a grant of this nature, it should be handed over to the provinces for educational purposes, letting them use it as they see best for either technical education or public schools. It is a terrible condition when one sees public schools closing and children not getting the privilege of learning to read and write, while the federal government is giving a grant for technical education. In my own village where we had five teachers, we have reduced the number to three and have. cut their salaries in half in order to keep the schools going, because there is very little money coming in from the municipality this year and there was very little last year.
These are some of the conditions as they exist out in the west, and if this legislation will give any relief to these people, I welcome it. I hope the relief work will begin at once, because, as I say, once the ground freezes up, very little work can be done at making roads, and that is practically the only work that can be given; otherwise the money will have to be paid out as direct relief.

There is another point: If this legislation passes it will be broadcast throughout the world that Canada is in such a situation, not only economically and socially but politically as well, that it requires the abolition of all parliamentary authority and the vesting of authority in a small body of men in order to cope with the situation. I ask the Prime Minister what effect this will have on the credit of this country among the nations of the world, when they see this legislation passed and then find that the situation has been exaggerated. I say the Prime Minister has exaggerated the seriousness of our political situation. He is quite right in providing for the relief of unemployment and in assisting the farmers of the west; I agree with him in that regard. Heroic measures are required to cope with these problems, but I do say that as far as the part of the bill is concerned which provides for the abolition of parliamentary authority, it should be withdrawn. Let me say here that I am absolutely opposed to any show of communism throughout this Dominion, but if the provisions of the criminal code or the other statutes of the country are not sufficient to meet any situation which may arise during the coming winter it is the duty of the Prime Minister or the Minister of Justice to bring in amendments to the criminal code in order to meet the situ-

About the only redeeming feature I see in the bill, Mr. Speaker, is section. 7, which provides for the expiration of the bill on March 31, 1932; that is the most satisfactory point, having regard to the taking away of the rights of parliament. Being one of the members from Toronto not on the government side, I have always cooperated with every member from Toronto in every unemployment relief measure brought before this house. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I intend to take only
a few moments of the time of the house, not in the hope of adding anything new but rather, if I may, to emphasize what has been said and to add my protest particularly with regard to the form of this legislation. Just a little while ago some hon. member said something about the argument with regard to the rights of the people having been exploded. I submit, Mr. Speaker, that the argument that parliament has the right and duty to limit the expenditure of public moneys is not exploded, and this House of Commons should not be asked to put its seal of approval on a bill which in effect does away with that power of limitation.
I submit that the precedents of the past in this Dominion, particularly during the time of the great war, to which reference has been made already, do not justify this action. Even in the early stages of the war, when the greatest uncertainty prevailed; when no one knew how long it would continue; when

Farm and Unemployment Relief
no one knew anything about the obligations which Canada might have to assume, a special session of the house was called and hon. members saw fit to place a limitation in that bill, even at that time of national crisis. The sum of 850,000,000 was expressly named, and as my hon. friend the ex-Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) pointed out to-night repeatedly, parliament was called upon during those four years to vote money many times, and a limitation was put in each bill.
There is really only one fundamental in connection with this legislation; it is this point, as to how far parliament should be asked to go in granting what is called a blank cheque and in going further and passing an omnibus bill at this time when it is so comparatively easy to call parliament together. I submit that one cannot do more than reiterate the principle already laid down, but I believe these protests should be allowed to pile up so that at least the government may see that we are in earnest and that the air of intolerance which has been displayed by hon. gentlemen opposite this evening may perhaps give way to some serious consideration of. the principle we are trying to establish.
The situation is simply this: there are three things in this bill which call for limitation. First there are the powers. It has been pointed out already by the ex-Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) that this bill gives to the government of Canada power to do anything which the parliament of Canada could do under the British North America Act. That is a pretty wide power; I do not believe it can be found in any bill which has been passed by this parliament since 1867. The next matter requiring limitation is the amount. The bill reads:
And, for the purposes aforesaid, may expend such moneys from the consolidated revenue fund as may be required.
There is absolutely no limit of any kind with regard to the amount. The third fundamental is that referred to so well by my hon. friend from Toronto West Centre (Mr. Factor) a few moments ago. Full power is given the governor in council to make orders and regulations-note the words-which shall have the force of law. They may amend the criminal code if they so desire. They may make orders and regulations for the carrying out of the purposes of this bill, which are not simply relief measures or to provide employment but which are for-the general omnibus words of the British North America Act-the peace, order and good government of Canada. As my hon. friend has pointed
out, not only have they power to make all orders and regulations necessary to exercise any one of those powers contained in the 29 subsections of section 91, but in addition to that they have the power to designate the courts before whom trials shall take place for violation of any of the regulations. If they like they may designate any departmental officer to try a man for an infringement of the regulations which they make under these very wide powers; they may designate a town councillor; they may designate a reeve of a municipality or a justice of the peace. And what may he do? The justice of the peace may try people, depriving them of the right of trial by jury. You will say that there is at least a limitation of penalty. Yes, there is. And that is the only limit in the bill apart from the fact that the act itself will expire on a certain date. The penalty limit is 81,000 and imprisonment for not more than three years, and that means that any one of these authorities designated by the governor in council, whether they happen to be judicial officers or not, may for a violation of the regulations made by the governor in council impose this fine and imprisonment. And they may decide that it shall be by summary conviction or by indictment.
I submit that these are provisions which offend against the fundamental principle I have indicated. Neither my right hon. friend nor any other member of the government except the Solicitor General (Mr. Dupre), to whom I shall refer in a moment, has spoken this evening to explain why these extraordinary measures are required. The Prime Minister has said that this blank cheque, this unlimited authorization as to amount, is needed because of the uncertainty of the situation. Well, I say that the situation could not be more uncertain than the situation in 1914, when an honoured and respected predecessor of my right hon. friend decided that the most he would ask for was 850,000,000. As my leader has said, if the Prime Minister would only ask for a specific amount to take care of contingencies there would be no cavilling about voting it. But what we object to is that we should be asked to give carte blanche, a blank cheque, an omnibus bill.
And that brings me to this other point. Not only does this legislation provide for the exercise of all these powers that are enumerated, but it groups together things that should not be grouped together in a bill of this kind. This is an omnibus enactment with regard to unemployment relief, farm relief, and peace,
Farm and Unemployment Relief

order and good government. The only member of the government who has spoken is the Solicitor General, and he says, "We challenge you to vote against it." Many a man has held a woman or a child in front of him and said, I challenge you to strike. It is very easy for hon. gentlemen to put the suffering and the hungry in the front line and challenge us to criticize this legislation, knowing as they do that it is for the relief of these people. The Solicitor General knows perfectly well that we are thinking more of unemployment relief than we are of the principle of the bill, but at the same time he cannot make with impunity the suggestion that we are doing anything more than our duty when we criticize that principle and what it stands for. Does he mean to say that because the object of this bill happens to be the relief of those who are in need, therefore there is to be no criticism of it? I say to him that he is in exactly the same position as a man who might stand behind a woman or a child and say, "I dare you to shoot." Of course we intend to vote for the bill, if my right hon. friend insists upon its going through in its present form. But we will not vote for it without making the strongest protest, not against the object of the bill, with which we are in full sympathy, but against its form. I venture to say that no man, if he were sitting on this side of the house, would be more vehement in his denunciation of the principle of this bill than the Prime Minister himself. If he were on this side he would stand up and say that he considered it his duty, in the interests of responsible institutions, to see to it that a measure of this kind should not be passed, vesting the government with any such powers. The shoe happens to be on the other foot, and as we are on the side where the hon. gentleman himself once was, we must bring to his attention and the attention of the people just what the implications of this bill are.
My hon. friend from Willow Bunch (Mi1. Donnelly) has referred to the administration of these relief moneys. I may say to the Prime Minister that, at least in some part3 of my constituency, that administration has not been satisfactory. My right hon. friend was good enough to rise and point out that it was not the federal government who were administering the measure. That is quite so.
I understand it is done through the provincial government and the municipalities. But we impressed upon the Prime Minister last session, as we impress upon him now, that since the federal parliament is voting the money it should have some say in its administration. I do not propose to mention a single case or to make any invidious com-
parisons, but I can give to my right hon. friend privately, or to his Minister of Labour if he wishes to have them, some illustrations of the cases I have in mind to show him that the relief money often does not reach those who need it. I know the object for which it was intended and for which the government took authority last fall. But the matter is too serious now, and the authority which my right hon, friend asks for is too great, for us not to make some provision that the money shall be properly expended and that it shall go to those for whom it is intended.
In closing, I repeat that my right hon. friend is going to far greater length than is necessary to carry out the object we have in view, and he is infringing upon a principle which I think, in his younger days at any rate, he would have observed, a principle which the people in my part of the country regard as very dear, because it was fought for in the early days of responsible government in the province of Nova Scotia. That principle is the accountability of the executive and the supervision by parliament over the executive with regard to the expenditure of money.
My hon. friend from Regina (Mr. Turnbull) spoke about the gratitude of the people for what the government had done. I do not think his leader, the Prime Minister, would particularly thank the hon. member for that remark. We must remember that this is the money of the taxpayers, the people of Canada, which is being voted. It is not the money of the government; and while we realize that the government are doing their duty in this matter, at the same time I do not think any question of gratitude need necessarily be raised in this house. Indeed, as the hon. member hastened to add, the administration was really only doing its duty. And because it is the money of the taxpayers of Canada which is being voted, I submit that my right hon. friend should put some limitation upon the provisions of this bill and should be more careful of the terms upon which he takes authority than appears from the provisions before us.

May I offer one or two words in reply to some of the observations that have been made in regard to this bill by hon. gentlemen opposite during the debate on the second reading. The hon. member for Shel-burne-Yarmouth (Mr. Ralston) has protested as vigorously as he can, and he certainly has emphasized and,. I think, exaggerated the possible consequences of the enactment of this legislation. The fears which he has ex-

Farm and Unemployment Relief
pressed have also been expressed by several members in the course of the debate this evening.
First and foremost, starting with my hon. friend from Quebec East (Mr. Lapointe), the hon. member for Toronto West Centre (Mr. Factor), my hon. friend from Shelburne-Yarmouth, the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Heenan) and one or two others, have uttered the same criticism in regard to the appearance in this bill of the words "peace, order and good government." There seems to be an idea that these words have been placed in this enactment for a sinister purpose. If the house will reflect for a moment I think it will realize that these words are the foundation of the authority of this parliament to pass such a measure. If the bill is not founded upon the theory that it is necessary to maintain peace, order and good government in Canada, then parliament would have no authority to pass it. Without these words the bill in the form in which it is enacted into law might be set aside when challenged in the courts. The judgments of the privy council during recent years have established most clearly that unless there is something in the nature of a national disaster, of plague, famine, or some national emergency, then parliament has no authority to legislate upon the subjects set out in this bill. After consultation with the law officers of the Department of Justice, we came to the conclusion that the best way to establish the authority of this parliament was to insert the clause which states that this measure is being passed for the maintenance of peace, order and good government in Canada. It is recognized that there is a national emergency. That question need not be argued, in view of the speeches made from every quarter of the house. We recognize this emergency by the adoption of these words from the British North America Act, and they were placed in the bill as the foundation of our authority to pass'such an enactment. They have nothing to do with the question of enforcement; they are merely a declaration to give us the jurisdiction which we know we have under the circumstances but of which we want to be sure.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I find myself wondering more and more why the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) and his colleagues should bring down such a beneficent measure as this in such an obnoxious form. There is no need to do this. My right hon. friend knows that our leader has indicated that he would agree to any amount named, be it $50,000,000, $75,-' 000,000 or $100,000,000. As long as there is a vote to give visibility to the purposes for which the money is to be used, and the amount named should not prove to be sufficient, governor general's warrants could be used. There is absolutely no reason why such an objectionable precedent should be created. With such a wide open door, hon. friends opposite say that is the way to restrict expenditure. It seems to me that the whole

country will be wanting to get into this relief vote when they know there is no limit to the amount.	[DOT]
There is no limit either upon the purposes for which this money is to be used. Almost anything but sheep stealing is to be permitted. There is no limit to the amount, scarcely any limit to the purposes, but it must stop on March 31. This afternoon the government was pluming itself because it was restoring to parliament certain rights in connection with the St. Lawrence, but this evening sacred rights are being taken away from parliament and given to the executive. Surely that is not a consistent attitude on the part of the government. If the record of this government during the last year had been such as to inspire confidence, it would not have been so bad, but there has not been a blunder between here and Makakanik which this government has not committed. Why should we allow them to adopt this course? True, it is not within our power to put them right; we will just have to let them go on their way, but not without a strong protest. They say grandiloquently: We dare not oppose it. We will not oppose it, but we will protest stoutly against it. As has been pointed out by the hon. member for Sheiburne-Yarmouth (Mr. Ralston), there were colonial difficulties in old Canada. I have often heard my father speak of 1837, the clergy reserves, and what not. These difficulties are bobbing up again under our present status, and this is another one. I would think the government were trying to borrow trouble. I do not see how they expect to deal with this relief matter better than they did last fall, especially when they start wrong. When they get off on the wrong foot, how are they going to get off on the right one? They are beginning with an indefinite expenditure-it may be $100,000,-OOO, $200,000,000, anything under the sun. That is not the way to run the affairs of this country at this time. I should have thought this was the worst time to open the door to such extravagance as may be possible. There are no conditions either under which the money is to be spent. As I listened to the hon. member for Willow Bunch (Mr. Donnelly), I knew he was not exaggerating the situation in any respect. I know what happened last fall. There is no use in talking about that too much, but we should avoid it rather than walk blindly into it again.
At times I have wondered, and I have asked myself many a time: Has this government really gone mad? It has not such a great distance to go, and thi3 is the latest

Farm and Unemployment Relief
bit of evidence to that effect. I give the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) full credit for starting out on the first of July with fine intentions. He did well; everybody was happy and the goose honked high all over the chamber. Now he precipitates this row unnecessarily at this time when we should have the very opposite conditions prevailing among us with reference to a relief bill of this nature. I believe he wants us to oppose it, bu,t we are not going to. Let him pass it, but we are on record as protesting against it as strongly as we know how.

I want
to draw the attention of the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) to the situation as I see it in the west and to one feature in particular which I think should be drawn to the attention of the government. Only this morning I received from the west a letter, a copy of which has been sent to the Prime Minister, and which I should like to put upon Hansard. My reason for doing this is that it will bring home to the house, perhaps more clearly than anything else, exactly what the situation is out there. I do not think the house fully appreciates how desperately hard up the people are. This letter is written by a doctor who has made a personal inspection of conditions in my - constituency. I may say that the whole of my constituency is in the dry belt area and I do not believe there is a single crop in it. This is not the first year there has been no crop; for thfee successive years they have been dried out, and four years ago in a large part of that district they were completely hailed out. Hon. members can imagine the financial situation of any business man who would try to carry on for four years without any income, but that is the position of the farmers in that part of the country. This letter was addressed to the Prime Minister and a copy sent to me: Rt. Hon. R. B. Bennett,
Ottawa, Ont., Can.
Dear Sir:-
Permit me to address you personally, re need of immediate relief in this particular part of the west, i.e. the rural municipality of Souris valley No. 7, in the constituency of Weyburn, Sask.
Should you read this, let me apologize for adding to your troubles, and also, thank you.
This municipality by the late census shows 2,200 people, about 420 families.
A day ago in company with our member for local house, Mr. R. S. Leslie, I visited in the short time at Mr. Leslie's disposal, foul-families adjacent to our hamlet.
At family No. 1, the conditions were; nine children, 12 years to 1 month old, children half clad, but all the clothes they have, for food.
two-thirds of a sack of flour, a little milk from two cows but the cows are now drying up as there is no feed, no fuel, no money, no crop, nothing to sell, this last sack of flour obtained from local municipality. To question "How do you expect to obtain coal and flour this winter?" they replied, "We do not know."
At the next neighbour 1) miles away, there are six children, seven years to two months old, also on last sack of flour, no potatoes, a little milk, no feed, no crop. Children will not be able to go to school after holidays for lack of clothes. Mother says she has made summer clothes for them out of flour sacks and pillow covers. Mother in her bare feet, has a pair of shoes but wants to keep them for church, shoes produced, were broken down and worn out. They put in 160 acres of crop, nothing in sight, potatoes will not grow, to question, "What do you expect to do this winter?" answered, "We do not know."
Third family, nine children, 19 years to 3 months, father 60 years of age, one of the pioneers here, hard workers all their lives, house and children neat and clean, have enough food to carry them along for about three weeks, after that they do not know what they will do, have never applied for help before, but they have no money, no credit, no crop in sight, no feed, for stock. Children have three miles to go to school, will have to stay home for lack of clothes this winter.
Fourth family, six children, nine years to six months, children not doing well, the mother says, thinks they do not get enough food, all dressed in old overalls made over from old pairs of the father, no crop in sight of any sort, do not know what they will do for the winter.
Thirty-six in these four families, all within radius of three and one-lialf miles, and out of 420 families in this municipality there are at least 300 of them in like position.
Have practised my profession in this municipality for sixteen years. I know the people and that they are honest, sober, and industrious.
Through no fault of their own they have reached this dire necessity.
Something must be done now. Flour and coal and food must be put in their possession at once, before -winter is on them, or there will be such a calamity as will be a lasting disgrace on all governing bodies of Canada.
Meetings of ratepayers are being held often, they get together and talk, and get nowheres. they are lost and desperate, and ready fuel for the agitation and the Red.
I realize what a difficult position the government must be in.
I realize living among these people in this stricken area much better than the government what we are up against.
And so I am begging you to strive for immediate action, that will result in something concrete, not promises.
Thanking you again for consideration of this letter.
Yours truly,

speechtext: The right hon. gentleman has put hi3 request most reasonably, but I must say I have considered the matter very carefully, and the more I have considered it the greater appears to be the difficulty, as it was in connection with old age pensions and several other statutes to which I could direct the attention of hon. members. There is no difference between the two, so far as I can see, having regard to the situation which has developed. Without taking up too much time I desire to say to my learned friends of the law that the real difficulty has been partly explained by what has been said to-night. In many instances apparently the provinces are unable to grapple with this situation, and the extent to which we must substitute the federal power for the provincial authority would seem to be a matter of the first magnitude and one with respect to which I certainly desire to proceed most guardedly, because of the general situation of Canada as a whole. I shall however think the matter over and speak to my right hon. friend in the morning.
